title: Cheap Drones, Dry Taps: The Iran War Opens a New Era of Water Infrastructure Risk
gist: Iran has turned Gulf desalination and power infrastructure into a credible deterrence lever against the US and its allies, with repeated drone and missile strikes on Kuwaiti, Bahraini, and Iranian water/power plants since Operation Epic Fury; the authors argue water is a uniquely fast-acting coercive target (days, not months) and that US/allied air-defense interceptor stocks are dangerously thin to hold the line.

themes.theme: Iran's water/energy infrastructure as a deterrence and coercion lever

insights.claim: Iranian Foreign Minister Aragchi warned Gulf states that renewed large-scale US strikes on Iran would be met with strikes on their critical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Signals Iran is explicitly weaponizing Gulf critical infrastructure as a deterrence threat against any renewed US military campaign.
insights.quote: Iranian Foreign Minister Aragchi recently made it clear to Gulf states that if the U.S. military renewed large-scale strikes on Iran, their critical infrastructure would be struck.

insights.claim: Iran and its adversaries have repeatedly struck Gulf desalination and power plants over roughly a five-month period, including Kuwaiti, Bahraini, and Iranian facilities, with the attacks continuing even after a ceasefire nominally took hold.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Establishes a live, recurring pattern of infrastructure targeting rather than a one-off incident, raising the odds of repeat attacks.
insights.quote: By July 21, Kuwait’s electricity ministry reported Iranian strikes on its power and desalination plants for a fourth consecutive night.
insights.locator: Kuwait first reported damage near a desalination plant

insights.claim: Current Gulf air defenses have so far prevented formal water rationing despite repeated strikes, but it is unclear whether they could withstand a sustained campaign of roughly 50 drones plus ballistic and cruise missiles fired daily at specific plant complexes.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Flags a plausible escalation scenario investors and insurers in Gulf infrastructure/desalination assets should stress-test against.
insights.quote: It is unclear whether they could do so against a more sustained Iranian strike campaign — for instance, a daily fire rate of 50 drones plus ballistic and cruise missiles directed at specific plant complexes.

themes.theme: Interceptor shortages as the binding constraint

insights.claim: US forces globally hold fewer than 1,000 Patriot missiles and roughly 250 THAAD interceptor rounds, a stockpile level a recent report estimates as thin relative to potential demand.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: A hard capacity constraint on US/allied ability to defend Gulf infrastructure through an extended Iranian strike campaign; watch Patriot/THAAD production ramp-up and reload contracts (RTX, Lockheed Martin) as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: A recent report estimates U.S. forces globally possess fewer than 1,000 Patriot missiles and approximately 250 THAAD interceptor rounds.
insights.locator: The shortage of U.S. and allied interceptor reloads

insights.claim: Ukraine's experience shows what happens once interceptor stocks run out: with high-end surface-to-air missiles depleted, Russia's ballistic missile barrages now inflict a heavy nightly toll on people and property.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Serves as a live proof case for what Gulf states risk if their own interceptor stocks are exhausted during a sustained Iranian campaign.
insights.quote: now that Ukrainian air defenders have run short of high-end surface-to-air missiles, Russia unleashes waves of ballistic missiles and the nightly toll in people and property is grim.
insights.locator: The best way to keep water systems online

insights.claim: Cheap drones costing about as much as a new American pickup truck can knock out a water system serving hundreds of thousands or millions of people from hundreds of kilometers away.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Highlights an extreme cost asymmetry between cheap offensive drones and expensive critical infrastructure/interceptors, a dynamic relevant to counter-drone investment theses.
insights.quote: A relatively small number of drones, each costing about as much as a typical new American pickup truck ($50,000 to $75,000, per the BBC), can shut down a water system supplying hundreds of thousands, or even millions of people.
insights.locator: The difference in today’s era of increasingly democratized

insights.claim: The authors call for cheaper, more numerous drone interceptors, and argue Ukrainian defense-tech manufacturers could scale to fill that gap if Gulf state capital is injected into their production.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Points to a specific capital-deployment opportunity: Gulf sovereign capital funding Ukrainian counter-drone manufacturing capacity.
insights.quote: Cheaper, more numerous drone interceptors are a must — a gap that Ukrainian defense tech providers could likely fill at scale with injections of Gulf State capital into their manufacturing bases.
insights.locator: Capital and construction capacity are already being mobilized

themes.theme: Water is a uniquely fast-acting coercive weapon

insights.claim: Unlike oil, gas, or food denial campaigns which take months to bite, disrupting a water system can trigger a major crisis within days, especially when combined with cyberattacks, a capability Iran credibly possesses.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Reframes water infrastructure as the fastest-acting coercive lever in the Gulf theater, ahead of energy or food denial, for scenario planning.
insights.quote: For water, on the other hand, disruptions could trigger a major crisis within days, especially if an adversary has thoroughly mapped the water system and combines multiple rounds of kinetic strikes with cyber-attacks
insights.locator: Water is unique as an instrument of coercion

insights.claim: Publicly available data suggests Qatar's ready water storage covers less than one week at average demand, while Saudi and Kuwaiti disclosures do not permit a reliable countrywide outage-endurance estimate.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Identifies Qatar as the most exposed Gulf state on water storage buffer, a relevant input for country-risk assessment.
insights.quote: Qatar’s ready storage appears consistent with less than one week of coverage at average demand
insights.locator: Once a desalination plant is knocked offline

insights.claim: Abu Dhabi has already built the Liwa/Al-Dhafra aquifer storage and recovery system, which can reportedly hold 90 days of water supply for the city by injecting excess desalinated water underground.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: A concrete resilience benchmark other Gulf states may now race to replicate; relevant to water-infrastructure engineering and construction firms serving the region.
insights.quote: Abu Dhabi has built the Liwa/Al-Dhafra aquifer storage and recovery system, which can reportedly store 90 days of supply for the city.
insights.locator: Injecting excess desalinated water into aquifers

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia can already reroute desalinated water between its Gulf and Red Sea coasts via a pipeline network exceeding 14,000 kilometers, though it lacks full cross-peninsula connectivity.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Existing pipeline redundancy gives Saudi Arabia more built-in resilience than smaller Gulf states like Kuwait or Qatar.
insights.quote: it can reroute water on both the Gulf and Red Sea coasts through a water pipeline network that is more than 14,000 km long.

insights.claim: The authors expect Saudi Arabia to pursue a 'hydrovascular grid' strategy modeled on the East-West Oil Pipeline to create true water connectivity between its Gulf and Red Sea coasts.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: A specific infrastructure investment theme to watch for in Saudi capital spending plans over the coming years.
insights.quote: it is likely that Saudi Arabia will consider a “hydrovascular grid” strategy that imitates the East-West Oil Pipeline and creates true connectivity between the Gulf and Red Sea Coasts

insights.claim: A large reverse-osmosis desalination facility can require 100 megawatts or more of power, comparable to a hyperscale data center or small city, meaning a strike on electrical infrastructure often disables water production as a secondary effect.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Ties Gulf water security directly to grid resilience and to a turbine/generator supply market already stretched by data-center demand.
insights.quote: a very large reverse osmosis facility can require 100 megawatts or more of power, in line with figures for Abu Dhabi’s Taweelah reverse-osmosis plant
insights.locator: Physical realities make legal assessments very complex

insights.claim: Kuwait's backup groundwater is brackish and requires treatment, making its secondary water supply itself vulnerable to strikes that cut electricity.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Kuwait has the least resilient fallback water supply among the Gulf states discussed, raising its relative vulnerability.
insights.quote: Kuwait’s groundwater resource is brackish and would require treatment to be fully potable, making its secondary water supply vulnerable to strikes that meaningfully reduce the country’s electricity supply.
insights.locator: Riyadh and Kuwait City have existing groundwater

insights.claim: Article 54(2) of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions bars attacks on drinking water installations intended to deny civilians their sustenance value, but the prohibition does not apply when a system solely sustains enemy armed forces, and a state may destroy its own water infrastructure under imperative military necessity.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Complicates any clean legal case against Iran's infrastructure strikes and underscores that legal assessment requires case-by-case factual analysis.
insights.quote: Article 54(2) of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions prohibits attacking drinking water installations when the attacks are intended to deny civilians the water’s sustenance value.
insights.locator: Physical Interdependence Complicates International Law Analysis

insights.claim: The authors add an eighth resilience step beyond the seven previously proposed (hardening, spare components, onsite power, plant dispersion, interconnected pipelines, expanded storage, dedicated air defenses): widespread civil defense training to build societal readiness and buy time for government responses.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Signals civil-defense and resilience training programs as a likely near-term policy priority across Gulf states.
insights.quote: we add an eighth critical step: widespread civil defense training to bolster societal readiness for infrastructure disruptions and buy time for governmental responses.
insights.locator: A March 2026 War on the Rocks analysis

insights.claim: Capital and construction capacity are already being mobilized to build energy bypass routes around the Strait of Hormuz, and the authors expect similar public-private investment in water pipeline networks, storage, and backup wellfields across GCC states.
insights.speaker: Gabriel Collins and Morgan D. Bazilian
insights.so_what: Points to an emerging Gulf capital-expenditure theme in water/energy resilience infrastructure requiring public-private partnership funding.
insights.quote: Capital and construction capacity are already being mobilized to build energy bypass options around the Strait of Hormuz.
